title: Data Center Is Fined $1.1 Million for Operating 62 Power Generators

reading.body:
This is a compliance failure at the physical layer of a deployment, not a failure of any model or output. The operators installed and ran 62 large natural gas generators at a Vineland data center site without the permits New Jersey requires for installation or operation. The equipment was in place and running before the state had authorised it, which is the plain form of the problem: infrastructure brought online outside the conditions it was built under.

The failure sits in the power supply, the part of a data center that must be permitted and inspected before the computing it feeds can be considered properly commissioned. Catching it would have taken a permit check at the point of installation and again before the generators were started, along with a comparison of what was actually built against what regulators had approved. The state found the generators only when inspectors visited in late July.

What is not established is intent. The federal lawsuit by homeowners is an allegation rather than a finding, and the fine is a penalty rather than a determination of why the permits were absent. The reporting also does not establish what computing the campus supports or whether the unpermitted generators were serving workloads that were already live.

reports.title: Data Center Is Fined $1.1 Million for Operating 62 Power Generators

summary:
New Jersey fined DataOne $1.07 million after state inspectors found 62 large natural gas generators at its Vineland data center site in late July. The generators, each 2,000 kilowatts and the size of tractor trailers, lacked required permits to be installed or operated. The fine, for violating the state's Air Pollution Control Act, is the largest ever issued to a New Jersey data center operator, officials said.

The planned 2.6 million square foot campus is slated for completion at the end of the year and would need 350 megawatts, enough to power a medium size city. Some of it is already in use. The project has drawn complaints, including a federal lawsuit by homeowners over persistent noise and violation orders from the Cumberland County Health Department for excessive noise. Governor Mikie Sherrill said such projects must benefit New Jersey communities.
